question.prompt:
In the cube \(ABCDEFGH\) with opposite vertices \(C\) and \(E,\) \(J\) and \(I\) are the midpoints of edges \(\overline{FB}\) and \(\overline{HD},\) respectively. Let \(R\) be the ratio of the area of the cross-section \(EJCI\) to the area of one of the faces of the cube. What is \(R^2?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2018_AMC_8_Q24_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
Let each cube edge have length \(s\). First identify the shape of the cross-section. Each of \(EJ,JC,CI,IE\) crosses a square face by one full edge length in one direction and half an edge length in the perpendicular direction. The Pythagorean theorem gives the same squared length \(s^2+(s/2)^2\) for all four sides. The cross-section is therefore a rhombus.

A rhombus has perpendicular diagonals, so its area is half the product of their lengths. Here those diagonals are \(EC\) and \(JI\). Since \(J\) and \(I\) are halfway up parallel cube edges, \(JI\) is a diagonal of the horizontal middle square, giving

\[
JI=\sqrt{s^2+s^2}=s\sqrt2.
\]

The segment \(EC\) is a body diagonal. Its horizontal projection is a face diagonal of length \(s\sqrt2\), and its vertical change is \(s\). Another use of the Pythagorean theorem gives

\[
EC=\sqrt{(s\sqrt2)^2+s^2}=s\sqrt3.
\]

The cross-section's area is \(\frac12(s\sqrt2)(s\sqrt3)=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}s^2\). A cube face has area \(s^2\), so

\[
R=\frac{\sqrt6}{2},\qquad R^2=\frac64=\boxed{\frac32},
\]

choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\). The diagonals are easier to measure than a perpendicular height within this tilted rhombus.
solutions.title: Justify rhombus shape and calculate its two diagonals
